These exercises follow the tasks on the slides of lecture 6, "Random forests in practice". Write your code in the empty chunks, and answer the questions in a sentence or two under each chunk. Section 4 goes beyond the slides.

## Setup

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(ranger)
library(simling)
```

## The data

`accent` comes from a simulated accent study in which 30 speakers, 15 with English as their L1 and 15 Italian learners of English, read 40 English words each. Each token has six acoustic measures: `vot` (ms), `vowel_ratio`, `rate` (syllables per second), `f0` (Hz), `h1h2` (dB) and `intensity` (dB).

```{r}
glimpse(accent)
```

The research question: can the acoustic measures tell an L1 English speaker from an Italian learner? `?accent` gives the true model. Leave it closed until you have finished section 3.

## 3. New speakers

### 3.1 Cross-validation by speaker

Complete the test set in this function, which fits a forest on four fifths of the speakers and predicts the other fifth, five times:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
set.seed(2)
folds <- distinct(accent, speaker, l1) |>
  mutate(fold = sample(rep(1:5, length.out = n())), .by = l1)
cv_speakers <- function(formula) {
  map(1:5, \(k) {
    train <- filter(accent, speaker %in% folds$speaker[folds$fold != k])
    test <- filter(accent, speaker %in% ___)
    m <- ranger(formula, data = train, num.trees = 500, seed = k)
    tibble(speaker = test$speaker, l1 = test$l1, pred = predict(m, test)$predictions)
  }) |> list_rbind()
}
```

Run `cv_speakers(f_all)`, and compute the accuracy on held-out speakers. `{konstats}` has a finished version of this function, `konstats::cv_speakers()`.

```{r}

```

